articles.author: RithyTep
articles.description:
I recently built KhmerCalendarBar, a macOS menu bar app that displays the Cambodian Chhankitek lunisolar calendar. Here's what I learned.

Cambodia uses a lunisolar calendar called Chhankitek alongside the Gregorian calendar. Public holidays like Khmer New Year, Pchum Ben, and Water Festival are determined by this system. I wanted quick access to Khmer dates without opening a browser.
SwiftUI with MenuBarExtra (.window style)
Swift Package Manager — zero external dependencies
create-dmg for styled DMG installers
The app uses a single CalendarViewModel (@MainActor, ObservableObject) that manages all state. Views are composable SwiftUI components:
KhmerCalendarBarApp
  └─ MenuBarExtra (popover)
       └─ PopoverContentView
            ├─ TodayHeaderView
            ├─ MonthNavigationView
            ├─ CalendarGridView
            ├─ HolidayListView
            ├─ YearOverviewView
            ├─ ClockView
            ├─ SettingsView
            └─ FooterView

The Khmer lunisolar calendar is complex:
Months alternate between 29 and 30 days
Intercalary months (Adhikameas) are added periodically
The Buddhist era year differs from Gregorian by 543
Each year has an animal cycle (like Chinese zodiac but different)
Waxing and waning phases are tracked per day
The conversion engine maps Gregorian dates to Khmer dates including lunar day, month name, era year, and animal cycle.
The menu bar shows Khmer date + time. Two timers handle updates:
Midnight timer — recalculates date at day change
Minute timer — updates time display every 30 seconds
MenuBarExtra with .window style gives you a proper popover
@MainActor on the ViewModel prevents threading issues
Timer-based updates need [weak self] to avoid retain cycles
UNUserNotificationCenter requires explicit authorization on macOS
create-dmg makes distribution easy without an Apple Developer account
Website: https://khmercalendarbar.rithytep.online


GitHub: https://github.com/RithyTep/KhmerCalendarBar


License: MIT
Contributions welcome!
articles.title: Building a macOS Menu Bar App for the Khmer Lunisolar Calendar with SwiftUI

articles.author: Ana Cunha
articles.description:
Today I wanted to print a markdown file and found out there was no straightforward way to do it from my code editor. Even though they have beautiful markdown previews, they won't let you print them.
That's when I found pandoc. Pandoc is a document converter that can turn markdown into PDF. It does this by converting markdown to LaTeX first, then using LaTeX to generate the PDF.
I don't miss struggling with LaTeX from my computer science student days, but it always produced beautiful documents (when I didn't mess anything up).
Here is the setup on macOS:
brew install pandoc
brew install basictex

After installing basictex, restart your terminal to get the LaTeX binaries in your path.
Then:
pandoc file.md -o file.pdf

That's it. PDFs from all your Markdown files.
articles.title: From Markdown to PDF

Most cloud recovery strategies assume something dangerous:

that logs, metadata, and audit trails remain trustworthy after an attack.
In real ransomware and APT incidents, attackers don’t stop at encrypting data.

They erase timelines, rewrite access trails, and poison audit logs.
Recovery still happens, but without certainty.
This article explores how IBM Cloud can be used to design verifiable recovery architectures, where restoration is based on cryptographic proof rather than trust.
Most environments rely on:
Snapshot-based backups

Centralized audit logs

Time-based restore points



These mechanisms fail under advanced attacks because:
Logs live in the same trust boundary as workloads

Metadata is flat and mutable

Recovery tools assume audit trails are truthful



Once attackers gain…
articles.title: Beyond Backups: Building Verifiable Cloud Recovery on IBM Cloud
